los.text: Describe the clinical presentation of haemoptysis and how this guides differential diagnosis, investigation, and initial management.
los.html:
Haemoptysis
  • Coughing up blood from the lower respiratory tract.
  • Distinguish from haematemesis (vomited, dark, acidic, food particles, GI history) and upper airway/nasopharyngeal bleeding (epistaxis, gum bleeding).
Quantify
  • Streaks vs frank blood
  • Massive haemoptysis (>~200–600 mL/24 h or any amount causing airway compromise/hypoxia/haemodynamic instability) = emergency (death by asphyxiation, not exsanguination).
Causes
  • Infection: bronchitis/pneumonia (rusty sputum: pneumococcus), TB (cavitation), bronchiectasis/CF, lung abscess, aspergilloma (in cavity).
  • Neoplasm: lung cancer (smoker >40), carcinoid, metastases.
  • Vascular: PE (pleuritic pain, breathlessness), pulmonary oedema (pink frothy), mitral stenosis, AVM (HHT), pulmonary hypertension.
  • Vasculitis/autoimmune: GPA (granulomatosis with polyangiitis: sinusitis, renal), Goodpasture's (anti-GBM: haemoptysis + nephritis), SLE.
  • Other: coagulopathy/anticoagulants, trauma, foreign body, iatrogenic (biopsy), cocaine, endometriosis (catamenial).
History guides differentials
  • Age
  • Smoking
  • Weight loss
  • Night sweats (TB, cancer)
  • Fever/purulent sputum (infection)
  • Chronic daily sputum (bronchiectasis)
  • Sudden breathlessness/pleuritic pain/leg swelling (PE)
  • Travel/TB contacts
  • Rash/haematuria/sinus symptoms (vasculitis)
  • Anticoagulants.
Investigations
  • Obs/sats, CXR (all), FBC, clotting, U&E, CRP, group and save, sputum MC&S and AFB ×3 (TB), cytology
  • CTPA (PE), CT chest with contrast (mass, bronchiectasis), bronchoscopy
  • Urine dipstick + ANCA/anti-GBM (vasculitis)
  • Echo (MS, pulmonary HTN).
Initial management
  • ABC
  • O₂
  • Position with bleeding lung down (protect good lung)
  • Large-bore access
  • Correct coagulopathy/stop anticoagulants
  • Tranexamic acid (nebulised or IV)
  • Antibiotics if infection
  • Urgent respiratory/IR input: bronchial artery embolisation
  • Bronchoscopy
  • Surgery
  • 2WW referral if suspected cancer (any unexplained haemoptysis ≥40).

los.text: Explain the clinical presentation of pulmonary embolism and how it is investigated and managed, including the patient’s experience of the condition.
los.html:
Clinical presentation
  • Sudden breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis (infarction), cough, syncope/collapse (massive PE), palpitations
  • Signs: tachypnoea (most common), tachycardia, hypoxia, low-grade fever, pleural rub, signs of DVT (unilateral leg swelling), raised JVP, hypotension/shock (massive), loud P2
  • May be silent or atypical (confusion, AF).
Investigation (NICE NG158)
  • Two-level Wells score: PE likely (>4) → CTPA immediately (interim anticoagulation if delay); PE unlikely (≤4) → D-dimer: if positive → CTPA; negative → PE excluded (consider PERC rule in very low-risk).
  • V/Q scan (renal impairment, contrast allergy, pregnancy (also low radiation to breast)).
  • Supporting: CXR (often normal; excludes others), ECG (sinus tachycardia; S1Q3T3, RBBB, right axis, T inversion V1–V4 = RV strain), ABG (type 1 failure, hypocapnia), troponin/BNP (RV strain: risk stratification), echo (RV dilatation; bedside in unstable), leg Doppler.
  • Risk stratification: PESI/sPESI, RV dysfunction, troponin → outpatient management (low risk) vs admission.
ManagementSee LO 7 (anticoagulation; thrombolysis if haemodynamically unstable).
Patient's experience
  • Sudden frightening breathlessness and chest pain (fear of dying)
  • Anxiety and loss of confidence afterwards
  • Worry about recurrence and travel
  • Burden of anticoagulation (bleeding risk, injections, monitoring, interactions)
  • Lifestyle changes
  • Investigations for cancer/thrombophilia
  • Post-PE syndrome (persistent breathlessness/exercise limitation in ~50%)
  • CTEPH (rare)
  • Psychological impact (PTSD)
  • Impact on work
  • Pregnancy/contraception planning (stop oestrogen-containing contraception).
  • Clear explanation, written information and follow-up (3-month review) help.

los.text: Describe the predisposing factors for venous thromboembolism and how these relate to clinical presentation, investigation, and management.
los.html:
Virchow's triadStasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability (see LO 24).
Predisposing factors
  • Major/transient: surgery (especially orthopaedic hip/knee, pelvic/abdominal cancer surgery), hospitalisation/immobility (bed rest >3 days), trauma/fractures, lower limb plaster cast, pregnancy and puerperium (highest postpartum), long-haul travel (>4 h), central venous catheters.
  • Persistent: active cancer (and chemotherapy, e.g. tamoxifen, thalidomide), previous VTE, thrombophilias (factor V Leiden, prothrombin mutation, protein C/S/antithrombin deficiency, antiphospholipid syndrome), obesity, age >60, oestrogen (COCP, HRT oral), heart failure, COPD, IBD, nephrotic syndrome, myeloproliferative disorders, PNH, smoking, varicose veins, dehydration, COVID-19, HIT.
Relation to presentation
  • DVT typically begins in calf veins (stasis in soleal sinuses/valve pockets) → propagates proximally → embolises to lungs
  • Post-op PE classically ~1–2 weeks after surgery
  • Cancer may present as unprovoked VTE (search for cancer with history, exam, bloods; CT only if symptoms).
Relation to investigation
  • Risk factors feed into Wells score (previous VTE, malignancy, immobilisation/surgery)
  • Thrombophilia testing only if unprovoked VTE + plan to stop anticoagulation and strong FHx (not routinely)
  • Antiphospholipid testing if unprovoked and considering stopping, or with pregnancy loss/arterial events.
Relation to management
  • Provoked (transient risk factor) → 3 months anticoagulation
  • Unprovoked → 3–6 months then consider long-term (balance bleeding risk: ORBIT/HAS-BLED)
  • Active cancer → DOAC or LMWH ≥6 months
  • Antiphospholipid syndrome → warfarin (not DOAC)
  • Pregnancy → LMWH (warfarin teratogenic; DOACs avoided)
  • Prevention: VTE risk assessment on admission → LMWH ± mechanical prophylaxis.

los.text: Explain how underlying pathology in thromboembolic disease leads to its clinical presentation.
los.html:
Thrombus formation
  • Venous thrombi (stasis) = red thrombi (fibrin and trapped RBCs, few platelets), often begin at valve cusps in deep calf veins
  • → propagate
  • → may detach.
EmbolisationFragment travels via IVC → right heart → pulmonary arteries and lodges according to size: saddle embolus (bifurcation of main pulmonary artery), lobar, segmental or subsegmental arteries.
Pathophysiological consequences → clinical features
  • Mechanical obstruction + vasoconstriction (thromboxane, serotonin from platelets) → ↑ pulmonary vascular resistance → ↑ RV afterload → RV dilatation and failure, ↑ RV wall tension and O₂ demand + ↓ coronary perfusion → RV ischaemia (troponin ↑), ventricular interdependence (septum bows into LV) → ↓ LV filling → ↓ cardiac output → hypotension, syncope, shock, PEA arrest (massive PE: >50% obstruction). Raised JVP, RV strain on ECG/echo.
  • Gas exchange: V/Q mismatch (dead space: ventilated but unperfused lung; redistribution of blood to other areas), right-to-left shunting (PFO, atelectasis) → hypoxaemia; hyperventilation (reflex, J receptors) → hypocapnia, tachypnoea, breathlessness.
  • Pulmonary infarction (~10%; peripheral emboli; lung has dual blood supply so infarction is uncommon unless pre-existing heart/lung disease): wedge-shaped haemorrhagic infarct with base on pleura → pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, pleural rub, small effusion, fever.
  • Small recurrent emboli → chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) (failed resolution, organisation of thrombi) → progressive breathlessness, RV failure.
Fate of emboliMost lyse (fibrinolysis) or organise; DVT → post-thrombotic syndrome.

los.text: Explain the physiological effects of acute and chronic pulmonary arterial hypertension and how these relate to clinical features, investigations, and management.
los.html:
Pulmonary hypertension (PH)Mean pulmonary arterial pressure >20 mmHg at rest on right heart catheterisation (2022 ESC definition; previously ≥25).
WHO/clinical classification
  • Group 1: pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) (idiopathic, heritable (BMPR2), drugs (anorexigens, dasatinib, methamphetamine), connective tissue disease (systemic sclerosis), HIV, portal hypertension, congenital heart disease (Eisenmenger))
  • Group 2: left heart disease (commonest: HFpEF/HFrEF, mitral/aortic valve disease)
  • Group 3: lung disease/hypoxia (COPD, ILD, OSA, altitude)
  • Group 4: CTEPH
  • Group 5: unclear/multifactorial (sarcoidosis, haematological).
Acute PH(massive PE)
  • Sudden ↑ PVR in a non-adapted thin-walled RV (can generate only ~40 mmHg acutely)
  • → acute RV failure, ↓ LV filling
  • → shock, collapse, raised JVP, RV dilatation on echo
  • → treat cause (thrombolysis), avoid excess fluids, vasopressors.
Chronic PH
  • Vascular remodelling (endothelial dysfunction: ↓ NO/prostacyclin, ↑ endothelin; smooth muscle proliferation, plexiform lesions, in situ thrombosis)
  • → progressive ↑ PVR
  • → RV hypertrophy (adaptation)
  • → later RV dilatation and failure (cor pulmonale).
Clinical features
  • Exertional breathlessness, fatigue, exertional syncope/presyncope, chest pain, palpitations, haemoptysis
  • Signs: loud P2, RV heave (parasternal), raised JVP with prominent a/v waves, tricuspid regurgitation (pansystolic murmur), peripheral oedema, hepatomegaly, ascites, cyanosis
  • Features of underlying disease (sclerodactyly, clubbing).
Investigations
  • Echo (screening: estimated PA systolic pressure, RV size/function, TR velocity)
  • ECG (RVH, right axis deviation, P pulmonale, RBBB)
  • CXR (enlarged pulmonary arteries, pruned peripheral vessels)
  • NT-proBNP
  • PFTs (↓ TLCO)
  • V/Q scan (to screen for CTEPH: mismatched defects)
  • CT/CTPA
  • HRCT
  • Autoimmune/HIV/LFTs
  • Sleep study
  • Right heart catheterisation (diagnostic gold standard; vasoreactivity testing).
Management
  • Refer to specialist PH centre
  • Treat underlying cause (Groups 2–3: optimise HF/lung disease, LTOT), diuretics, oxygen, anticoagulation (CTEPH, some PAH), exercise rehab
  • PAH-specific: endothelin receptor antagonists (bosentan, ambrisentan, macitentan)
  • PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil)
  • Riociguat (sGC stimulator: CTEPH)
  • Prostacyclin analogues (IV epoprostenol, selexipag)
  • High-dose CCBs (vasoreactive responders only)
  • CTEPH → pulmonary endarterectomy (Papworth), balloon pulmonary angioplasty
  • Lung transplant
  • Avoid pregnancy (high mortality).

los.text: Explain the physiological effects of acute and chronic pulmonary arterial hypertension and how these relate to clinical features, investigations, and management including radiological investigations
sessions: Radiological presentations on causes of haemoptysis
los.html:
Radiological investigations in PH and haemoptysis
  • CXR: enlarged central pulmonary arteries (prominent hila), peripheral "pruning" (oligaemic lung fields), cardiomegaly with RV/RA enlargement (filling of retrosternal space on lateral), signs of underlying disease (hyperinflation, fibrosis, pulmonary venous congestion in left heart disease).
  • CT pulmonary angiography: main pulmonary artery diameter ≥29 mm (or larger than ascending aorta: PA:Ao ratio >1), RV dilatation (RV:LV ratio >1), septal flattening/bowing, contrast reflux into IVC/hepatic veins, acute PE (filling defects; "polo mint" sign) vs chronic thromboembolic disease (eccentric wall-adherent thrombi, webs, bands, mosaic perfusion, bronchial artery collaterals).
  • HRCT: interstitial lung disease, emphysema, centrilobular ground glass (pulmonary veno-occlusive disease), mosaic attenuation.
  • V/Q (SPECT) scan: screening test of choice for CTEPH (normal scan excludes it; mismatched segmental perfusion defects suggest it).
  • Echo: estimates PA pressure (TR jet velocity), RV function (TAPSE), pericardial effusion (poor prognosis).
  • Cardiac MRI: RV volume and function, prognosis.
  • Pulmonary angiography/right heart catheterisation: confirmation, haemodynamics, CTEPH operability.
Haemoptysis imagingCXR → CT chest with contrast (CT angiography) for source localisation (tumour, bronchiectasis, aspergilloma, cavity, AVM) and planning bronchial artery embolisation (bronchial arteries are the source of most massive haemoptysis).
LinkImaging identifies cause (PH group), severity (RV failure), and guides management (thrombolysis/anticoagulation, endarterectomy, embolisation, PAH therapy).

los.text: Explain the principles of management of pulmonary embolism, including acute treatment and longer-term anticoagulation.
los.html:
Acute treatment
  • Haemodynamically unstable (massive/high-risk PE: SBP <90): systemic thrombolysis (alteplase 10 mg bolus then 90 mg over 2 h, or 50 mg bolus in cardiac arrest) unless contraindicated; alternatives: surgical embolectomy, catheter-directed therapy; unfractionated heparin (can be stopped/reversed quickly); supportive care (O₂, cautious fluids, vasopressors), ECMO.
  • Haemodynamically stable: start anticoagulation as soon as PE suspected (if not contraindicated): DOAC (apixaban or rivaroxaban: no LMWH lead-in needed) first line; or LMWH then dabigatran/edoxaban, or LMWH + warfarin (INR 2–3, stop LMWH when INR ≥2 for 24 h). LMWH for pregnancy and (alternative) cancer. UFH in severe renal impairment (CrCl <15) or high bleeding risk/planned thrombolysis.
  • Intermediate-high risk (RV dysfunction + ↑ troponin): anticoagulate, monitor closely, rescue thrombolysis if deteriorates.
  • Low risk (sPESI 0): outpatient (ambulatory) management with DOAC and follow-up.
  • IVC filter only if anticoagulation contraindicated/recurrent PE despite anticoagulation (remove when possible).
Longer-term anticoagulation
  • Provoked PE (major transient risk factor) → 3 months.
  • Unprovoked → at least 3 months, then consider long-term (indefinite) if bleeding risk acceptable (assess with ORBIT; patient preference); reduced-dose apixaban/rivaroxaban for extended phase.
  • Active cancer → 3–6 months+ (as long as cancer active) with DOAC or LMWH.
  • Antiphospholipid syndrome → warfarin long term.
  • Review at 3 months; consider cancer symptoms, thrombophilia (selective), CTEPH screening if persistent breathlessness (echo/V/Q).
CounsellingBleeding signs, adherence, interactions (NSAIDs, antibiotics with warfarin), alert card, contraception (avoid oestrogen), travel advice.

los.text: Apply the Brief Intervention model to Smoking Cessation
los.html:
Brief intervention
  • Short, opportunistic advice (30 seconds to a few minutes) delivered to smokers in routine consultations
  • Doubles quit rates when combined with support.
Very Brief Advice (VBA) – "3 As" / "Ask, Advise, Act"(NCSCT)
  • ASK and record smoking status (and vaping).
  • ADVISE on the best way to quit: "The best way of stopping smoking is with a combination of medication and specialist support" (non-judgemental; personalise: link to their health problem, e.g. COPD, PE risk with COCP).
  • ACT on the response: offer referral to specialist stop smoking service (Help Me Quit in Wales) and/or prescribe pharmacotherapy; if not ready, keep the door open, provide information.
5 As model (Ask, Advise, Assess readiness, Assist, Arrange follow-up) is the older framework.
Pharmacotherapy
  • NRT (combination: patch + short-acting gum/inhalator/spray)
  • Varenicline (α4β2 nicotinic partial agonist: most effective; nausea, vivid dreams) (reintroduced in UK 2024)
  • Cytisine/cytisinicline (similar mechanism)
  • Bupropion
  • e-cigarettes/vapes as a quitting aid (less harmful than smoking; NICE supports for adults trying to quit).
Specialist supportBehavioural support + medication → quit rates ~4× higher than willpower alone.
Very ill/hospitalOpt-out models, NRT on admission, inpatient tobacco dependence services.

los.text: (OFG 1) Make the care of patients their first concern, applying their knowledge and skills in a competent, ethical and professional manner and taking responsibility for their own actions in complex and uncertain situations.
los.html:
• Outcomes for Graduates (GMC 2018)
  • OFG 1: Professional values and behaviours: newly qualified doctors must make the care of patients their first concern
  • Applying knowledge and skills competently
  • Ethically and professionally
  • and take responsibility for their own actions in complex and uncertain situations.
In practice
  • Patient-centred care: dignity, respect, privacy, involve patients in decisions, act in their best interests, advocate for them.
  • Competence: keep knowledge/skills up to date (CPD), work within competence, evidence-based care, recognise and manage uncertainty (safety-netting, seeking senior input).
  • Ethical and professional conduct: honesty and integrity (probity), confidentiality, consent, avoid conflicts of interest, appropriate boundaries.
  • Responsibility: own errors (duty of candour: apologise, explain, put right), reflect and learn, report incidents (Datix), raise concerns about patient safety (whistleblowing), maintain own health (fitness to practise), act on concerns about colleagues.
  • Complex/uncertain situations: multimorbidity, conflicting priorities, incomplete information → structured decision-making, documentation of reasoning, shared decisions, escalation.
GMC Good Medical Practice (2024)Domains: knowledge, skills and development; patients, partnership and communication; colleagues, culture and safety; trust and professionalism.

los.text: (OFG2c) Summarise the current ethical dilemmas in medical science and healthcare practice; the ethical issues that can arise in everyday clinical decision-making; and apply ethical reasoning to situations which may be encountered in the first years after graduation.
los.html:
Current ethical dilemmas(medical science and healthcare)
  • End of life: assisted dying (Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill progressing in England and Wales; not yet law), withdrawal of treatment, DNACPR, futility, palliative sedation.
  • Resource allocation: rationing (NICE/QALYs), waiting lists, expensive drugs (gene therapies, anti-amyloid antibodies), COVID-era triage.
  • Genomics and new technologies: gene editing (CRISPR), embryo research, genetic privacy, AI in healthcare (accountability, bias, consent, data use).
  • Reproductive ethics: abortion, IVF/embryo selection, surrogacy, mitochondrial donation.
  • Consent and capacity: Montgomery, children (Gillick), mental capacity, coercion.
  • Confidentiality vs public interest: DVLA, safeguarding, infectious disease, genetic information to relatives.
  • Vaccine hesitancy and mandates, public health vs individual liberty.
  • Organ donation (opt-out, DCD), conscientious objection, gender-affirming care for young people (Cass Review), industrial action, climate responsibility.
Everyday clinical ethics
  • Consent for routine procedures
  • Truth-telling
  • Confidentiality in shared spaces
  • Treating patients who refuse treatment
  • Respecting autonomy vs safety (frail elderly)
  • Managing limited time/beds fairly
  • Honesty about errors
  • Boundaries.
Ethical reasoning tools
  • Four principles (autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice)
  • Four-quadrant approach (Jonsen: medical indications, patient preferences, quality of life, contextual features)
  • Consequentialism vs deontology vs virtue ethics
  • Law and GMC guidance
  • Seek senior/ethics committee advice
  • Document reasoning.

los.text: (OFG2h) Recognise and acknowledge their own personal and professional limits and seek help from colleagues and supervisors when necessary, including when they feel that patient safety may be compromised.
los.html:
OFG 2h: recognise limits and seek help
  • Know your scope of competence (as FY1: e.g. prescribing, procedures, decisions requiring senior input) and the limits of your knowledge.
  • Seek help early from seniors/colleagues/supervisors when: unsure of diagnosis/management, patient deteriorating (NEWS2 triggers), unfamiliar procedure, ethical/legal uncertainty, emotionally overwhelmed, tired/unwell, or patient safety may be compromised.
  • Escalation: structured communication (SBAR), graded assertiveness (PACE: Probe, Alert, Challenge, Emergency), use of chain of command if concerns not addressed, clinical incident reporting.
  • Human factors: fatigue (HALT: Hungry, Angry, Late, Tired), cognitive biases, workload; take breaks.
  • Own health: register with a GP, don't self-prescribe, seek occupational health/practitioner health support, recognise burnout; fitness to practise responsibility.
  • Raising concerns (GMC Raising and acting on concerns about patient safety): duty to act when you believe patient safety, dignity or comfort is compromised (including by colleagues, systems or resources).
Safe culture"it's OK to ask", no blame for seeking help, reflective practice, supervision.

los.text: (OFG2m) Act appropriately, with an inclusive approach, towards patients and colleagues.
los.html:
OFG 2m: act appropriately with an inclusive approach
  • Treat all patients and colleagues fairly and with respect, without discrimination on grounds of protected characteristics (Equality Act 2010: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage/civil partnership, pregnancy/maternity, race, religion/belief, sex, sexual orientation) or other factors (socioeconomic status, lifestyle, immigration status).
  • Recognise and challenge discrimination, bullying, harassment and unconscious bias (in self and others); be aware of health inequalities and structural racism (e.g. pulse oximeter inaccuracy in darker skin, maternal mortality disparities).
  • Make reasonable adjustments (interpreters, accessible information, learning disability passports, hearing loops), use inclusive language (names, pronouns), culturally competent care.
  • Colleagues: respectful teamwork across professions, support colleagues (including those from different backgrounds, IMGs), speak up about inappropriate behaviour (sexual harassment: GMC 2024 guidance), equal opportunities.
  • Professional boundaries and conduct online/social media.
WhyImproves trust, communication, patient outcomes, team performance and wellbeing; legal and professional duty (GMC Good Medical Practice).

los.text: Explain the pathophysiology, risk factors, and clinical presentation of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) in a way any patient can understand
los.html:
Lay explanation of COPD
  • "COPD stands for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
  • It's a long-term lung condition where the airways (breathing tubes) become narrowed and inflamed and the tiny air sacs at the ends of the airways (where oxygen goes into the blood) become damaged.
  • This makes it harder to breathe out fully, so air gets trapped, and you feel breathless, especially when you're active."
Cause/risk factors
  • "The main cause is smoking: the chemicals irritate and damage the lungs over many years.
  • Other causes include breathing in dust
  • Fumes or chemicals at work
  • Smoke from wood or coal fires
  • and rarely a genetic condition (alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency).
  • Air pollution and childhood chest infections can add to the risk."
Symptoms
  • "Breathlessness that slowly gets worse, a long-term cough, bringing up phlegm, wheezing, frequent chest infections, and sometimes tiredness or weight loss.
  • Some people have flare-ups when symptoms suddenly get worse, often triggered by infections."
Key messages
  • The damage can't be fully reversed, but stopping smoking is the most important thing to slow it down
  • Treatments (inhalers, pulmonary rehab, vaccines) help symptoms and reduce flare-ups
  • You can still live well.
Communication skills
  • Check prior knowledge (ICE)
  • Chunk and check
  • Avoid jargon
  • Use analogies (e.g. "like breathing out through a narrow straw", "balloons that lose their stretch")
  • Diagrams
  • Teach-back
  • Written information (Asthma + Lung UK).

los.text: Apply MI techniques to discuss the role of lifestyle modifications (e.g. smoking cessation, exercise, diet) in managing COPD and improving patient outcomes
los.html:
Motivational interviewing (MI)Collaborative, person-centred conversation to strengthen a person's own motivation and commitment to change (Miller & Rollnick).
Spirit (PACE)Partnership, Acceptance (autonomy, empathy, affirmation), Compassion, Evocation (draw out their reasons).
Core skills (OARS)
  • Open questions ("What do you think about your smoking now?")
  • Affirmations ("You've managed to cut down before; that took real effort.")
  • Reflective listening ("It sounds like you're worried about getting more breathless but smoking helps you cope with stress.")
  • Summaries.
Processes
  • Engaging
  • → focusing (agree topic: smoking, exercise, diet)
  • → evoking (elicit change talk: Desire, Ability, Reasons, Need (DARN), Commitment, Activation, Taking steps)
  • → planning.
Techniques
  • Importance and confidence rulers ("On a scale of 0–10, how important is stopping smoking to you? Why a 6 and not a 3?")
  • Decisional balance (pros/cons of change)
  • Exploring ambivalence
  • Rolling with resistance/discord (don't argue; avoid the "righting reflex")
  • Elicit–provide–elicit for information
  • Support self-efficacy.
COPD lifestyle topics
  • Smoking cessation (biggest impact; offer VBA + referral + medication)
  • Pulmonary rehabilitation/exercise (improves breathlessness, QoL, reduces admissions)
  • Healthy diet/weight (malnutrition in advanced COPD; obesity)
  • Vaccinations
  • Inhaler technique/adherence
  • Managing exacerbations (rescue packs, action plan)
  • Alcohol.
CloseSummarise, agree realistic goals (SMART), follow-up, respect autonomy if not ready.

los.text: Interpret arterial blood gas (ABG) results, apply clinical reasoning to identify the likely causes of abnormalities through case-based discussions
los.html:
• Systematic ABG interpretation:
1. Patient/contextClinical state, FiO₂, arterial vs venous.
2. Oxygenation
  • PaO₂ (normal 10–13 kPa on air)
  • <8 kPa = respiratory failure
  • Compare with FiO₂ (expected PaO₂ ≈ FiO₂(%) − 10)
  • A–a gradient.
3. pH<7.35 acidaemia, >7.45 alkalaemia.
4. PaCO₂(4.7–6.0 kPa)↑ = respiratory acidosis/compensation for alkalosis; ↓ = respiratory alkalosis/compensation for acidosis.
5HCO₃⁻ (22–26) / base excess (−2 to +2): ↓ = metabolic acidosis; ↑ = metabolic alkalosis.
6Primary disorder and compensation (does the pH fit? mixed?).
7Anion gap (metabolic acidosis), lactate, glucose, electrolytes (K⁺, Na⁺, Cl⁻), Hb, COHb.
  • Case patterns:
ABGInterpretationLikely causes
↓PaO₂, ↓/normal PaCO₂, ↑pHType 1 respiratory failure + respiratory alkalosisPE, pneumonia, asthma (early), pulmonary oedema
↓PaO₂, ↑PaCO₂, ↓pH, normal HCO₃⁻Acute type 2 respiratory failure (acute respiratory acidosis)Opioid overdose, exhausted asthmatic, COPD exacerbation (if no prior chronic), neuromuscular
↑PaCO₂, ↑HCO₃⁻, normal pHChronic compensated respiratory acidosisStable COPD CO₂ retainer, OHS
↑PaCO₂, ↑HCO₃⁻, ↓pHAcute-on-chronic type 2 failureCOPD exacerbation → NIV if pH <7.35
↓pH, ↓HCO₃⁻, ↓PaCO₂, high anion gapMetabolic acidosis with respiratory compensationDKA, lactic acidosis (sepsis, ischaemia), AKI, toxins (methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylate)
↓pH, ↓HCO₃⁻, normal anion gap (↑Cl⁻)Hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosisDiarrhoea, RTA, Addison's, excess saline
↑pH, ↑HCO₃⁻, ↑PaCO₂ (compensation), ↓K⁺, ↓Cl⁻Metabolic alkalosisVomiting, diuretics, Conn's
↑pH, ↓PaCO₂, normal HCO₃⁻Acute respiratory alkalosisAnxiety/hyperventilation, pain, PE, early salicylate
Normal PaO₂ + ↑COHb, headacheCO poisoning

los.text: Elicit a focused cardiovascular and respiratory history and analyse presenting symptoms to formulate appropriate differential diagnoses in a patient with dyspnoea (breathlessness)
sessions: Cardio-respiratory history and examination with a focus on occupational illnesses
los.html:
Breathlessness history
  • Onset and time course: sudden (PE, pneumothorax, MI, anaphylaxis, foreign body), hours–days (pneumonia, asthma/COPD exacerbation, pulmonary oedema, effusion), weeks–months (anaemia, effusion, cancer, ILD, HF), chronic progressive (COPD, ILD, HF, pulmonary hypertension, obesity/deconditioning, neuromuscular).
  • Severity/exercise tolerance: MRC dyspnoea scale (1–5), stairs/distance, impact on ADLs; at rest?
  • Pattern: orthopnoea (HF, diaphragm weakness), PND (HF), episodic/variable/nocturnal (asthma), positional, exertional.
  • Associated: chest pain (pleuritic: PE, pneumothorax, pneumonia; central/crushing: ACS), cough and sputum (colour, volume), haemoptysis, wheeze, fever, palpitations (arrhythmia), syncope (PE, AS, arrhythmia), ankle swelling, weight change, night sweats.
  • Cardiac risk factors, previous lung/heart disease, VTE risk factors.
  • Drug history: β-blockers (bronchospasm), amiodarone/methotrexate/nitrofurantoin (fibrosis), ACEi (cough), new drugs (anaphylaxis).
  • Smoking (pack-years), occupation (ICM Year 2 › Respiratory › LO 11), pets/birds, travel, alcohol.
  • FH: asthma/atopy, α1-antitrypsin, cardiomyopathy, VTE.
Differential by systemRespiratory (asthma, COPD, pneumonia, ILD, effusion, pneumothorax, PE, cancer, bronchiectasis), cardiac (HF, ACS, arrhythmia, valve disease, pericardial effusion), other (anaemia, metabolic acidosis, anxiety/dysfunctional breathing, obesity, deconditioning, neuromuscular, thyroid).

los.text: Recognise the relevance of occupational exposures in a patient history and link potential risk factors to differential diagnoses
sessions: Cardio-respiratory history and examination with a focus on occupational illnesses
los.html:
Why occupational history matters
  • Many lung diseases are work-related, often preventable, compensable (Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit), and early removal from exposure can improve outcome
  • Long latency means asking about all previous jobs ("What jobs have you done since leaving school?").
Ask
  • Job titles and actual tasks
  • Materials handled
  • Dusts/fumes/chemicals
  • PPE and ventilation
  • Duration and intensity
  • Symptoms better on days off/holidays (asthma)
  • Similar symptoms in co-workers
  • Hobbies (pigeons, woodwork).
Exposure (occupations)Disease
Asbestos (shipbuilding (Swansea/Cardiff docks), construction, plumbers, electricians, demolition, boilermakers, laggers; family members washing clothes)Pleural plaques, diffuse pleural thickening, asbestosis (basal fibrosis), mesothelioma, lung cancer
Coal dust (miners: South Wales valleys)Coal workers' pneumoconiosis, progressive massive fibrosis, COPD
Silica (quarrying, stonemasons, sandblasting, engineered stone worktops, foundry)Silicosis (upper zone nodules, eggshell calcification of hilar nodes), ↑ TB, lung cancer
Isocyanates (spray painters), flour (bakers), wood dust, latex (healthcare), solder/colophony, laboratory animals, cleaning agentsOccupational asthma
Organic antigens (farmers: mouldy hay; bird fanciers; mushroom workers)Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (extrinsic allergic alveolitis)
Beryllium (aerospace, electronics)Berylliosis (sarcoid-like)
Cotton (byssinosis), fumes/gases (chlorine, welding fumes), smoking + dustsCOPD, metal fume fever, acute lung injury
Healthcare/prisons/migrantsTB
  • Link: e.g. retired dock worker with breathlessness + pleural effusion → mesothelioma
    • baker with work-related wheeze → occupational asthma (serial PEF at work: OASYS; refer early)
    • notify RIDDOR
    • compensation advice.

los.text: Perform focused cardiovascular and respiratory examinations and interpret key findings to support diagnostic reasoning in a patient with breathlessness
sessions: Cardio-respiratory history and examination with a focus on occupational illnesses
los.html:
Focused cardiovascular exam(ICM Year 2 › Cardiovascular › LO 3)Pulse (rate/rhythm: AF), BP, JVP, apex (displaced), heaves/thrills, heart sounds (S3, murmurs), lung bases, peripheral/sacral oedema.
Focused respiratory exam(ICM Year 2 › Respiratory › LO 1)RR, sats, accessory muscles, clubbing, tar staining, flap, trachea, expansion, percussion, breath sounds, added sounds, vocal resonance, calves.
Interpreting key findings in breathlessness
FindingsSupports
↑ JVP, displaced apex, S3, bibasal fine crackles, pitting oedemaHeart failure
Irregularly irregular pulseAF (cause or consequence)
Ejection systolic murmur, slow-rising pulseAortic stenosis
Wheeze, prolonged expiration, hyperinflation, tar staining, pursed lipsCOPD/asthma
Focal bronchial breathing, dullness, crackles, feverPneumonia
Stony dullness, ↓ breath sounds, ↓ vocal resonancePleural effusion
Hyper-resonance, absent breath sounds, deviated tracheaPneumothorax
Clubbing + fine end-inspiratory "velcro" cracklesILD/pulmonary fibrosis (asbestosis)
Tachycardia, tachypnoea, clear chest, unilateral swollen calfPE
Loud P2, RV heave, ↑ JVP with clear lungsPulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale
Pallor, flow murmurAnaemia
  • Next steps: sats/ABG, ECG, CXR, bloods (FBC, BNP, D-dimer if indicated, troponin), spirometry, echo, CT.

los.text: Describe the course of emboli (mobile blood clots) and the pathological effects in both the venous and arterial circulations.
los.html:
Venous emboli(from DVT in leg/pelvic veins, or right heart)
  • Travel IVC → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary trunk
  • → lodge in pulmonary arteries (size-dependent: saddle, lobar, segmental)
  • → PE effects: ↑ PVR, RV strain/failure, V/Q mismatch/hypoxia, pulmonary infarction (only ~10%: dual supply from bronchial arteries), sudden death (massive).
  • The lungs act as a filter protecting the systemic circulation.
Paradoxical embolismVenous embolus crosses into the systemic arterial circulation via a right-to-left shunt (patent foramen ovale, ASD, pulmonary AVM) → stroke or limb ischaemia (consider in young cryptogenic stroke).
Arterial (systemic) emboli(from left atrium (AF), LV mural thrombus (post-MI, dilated cardiomyopathy), valve vegetations (endocarditis), prosthetic valves, atherosclerotic plaques (aorta, carotid), aneurysms)
  • Travel to end arteries/narrow points: brain (stroke/TIA: MCA most common)
  • Limbs (acute limb ischaemia: femoral/popliteal bifurcations)
  • Mesenteric (acute mesenteric ischaemia: SMA)
  • Kidneys (renal infarct)
  • Spleen
  • Retina (amaurosis fugax, CRAO) → infarction (necrosis) because most organs have limited collaterals.
Effects depend onSize of embolus, organ's collateral supply/dual blood supply (lung, liver protected), tissue vulnerability (brain, heart: high metabolic demand), speed of occlusion.

los.text: Define the term 'bronchopulmonary segment' and explain its importance.
los.html:
Bronchopulmonary segment
  • The largest subdivision of a lobe
  • a pyramid-shaped portion of lung with its apex at the hilum and base at the pleural surface, supplied by its own segmental (tertiary) bronchus and segmental branch of the pulmonary artery, which run centrally together
  • Separated from adjacent segments by connective tissue septa
  • Drained by intersegmental pulmonary veins running between segments (in the septa).
Number
  • 10 on the right (upper 3: apical, posterior, anterior; middle 2: lateral, medial; lower 5: superior, medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal, posterior basal)
  • 8–10 on the left (apicoposterior combined, anteromedial basal combined; lingula: superior and inferior).
Importance
  • Surgical resection (segmentectomy) of diseased segments (localised bronchiectasis, small cancers, TB) with minimal bleeding/air leak, preserving lung function.
  • Localisation of disease on imaging and bronchoscopy; segmental collapse/consolidation patterns.
  • Aspiration pneumonia location by posture: supine → posterior segment of right upper lobe and superior (apical) segment of right lower lobe; upright → basal segments of right lower lobe.
  • Postural drainage physiotherapy positions for each segment (bronchiectasis/CF).
  • Infarcts/emboli correspond to arterial segments.

los.text: Identify parts of the pulmonary circulation to the second division of great vessels (very briefly).
los.html:
Pulmonary circulation (to second division)
  • Pulmonary trunk: arises from the right ventricle (conus arteriosus), runs up and back to the left, lying anterior then left of the ascending aorta, within the pericardium; divides at the level of T5/sternal angle (under aortic arch) into:
  • Right pulmonary artery: longer, passes horizontally behind the ascending aorta and SVC and in front of the right main bronchus to the right hilum → divides into upper lobe (truncus anterior) and interlobar branches (→ middle and lower lobes).
  • Left pulmonary artery: shorter, passes anterior to descending aorta and over the left main bronchus to the left hilum; connected to the aortic arch by the ligamentum arteriosum (remnant of ductus arteriosus; left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks around it) → lobar branches.
  • Branches follow the bronchi (lobar → segmental arteries).
Pulmonary veinsUsually four (superior and inferior on each side) → left atrium (oxygenated blood).
Hilum relations
  • Right: bronchus posterior and superior (eparterial bronchus to upper lobe above artery)
  • Left: artery superior, bronchus below/behind, veins anterior and inferior.

los.text: Describe the blood of the lungs.
los.html:
Blood supply of the lungs(dual supply)
  • Pulmonary circulation (functional): deoxygenated blood from RV via pulmonary arteries → alveolar capillaries (gas exchange) → oxygenated blood via pulmonary veins → LA. Receives entire cardiac output at low pressure (~25/10 mmHg) and low resistance.
  • Bronchial circulation (nutritive): oxygenated blood from bronchial arteries (left: two from descending thoracic aorta; right: usually one from the 3rd posterior intercostal artery or upper left bronchial artery) → supply bronchi, bronchioles (to respiratory bronchioles), visceral pleura, connective tissue, lymph nodes, vasa vasorum of pulmonary vessels; ~1–2% of cardiac output at systemic pressure.
Venous drainage
  • Bronchial veins (from proximal bronchi) → azygos (right) and accessory hemiazygos (left)
  • Much bronchial blood from distal airways drains into pulmonary veins (physiological shunt → slight desaturation of arterial blood).
LymphaticsSuperficial (subpleural) and deep plexuses → bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes → tracheobronchial nodes → bronchomediastinal trunks.

los.text: List the differences between the pulmonary circulation and the bronchial circulation, and recognise the links between them
los.html:
Pulmonary circulationBronchial circulation
OriginRight ventricle (pulmonary trunk)Systemic: descending aorta / intercostal arteries
Blood carriedDeoxygenated (arterial side)Oxygenated
FunctionGas exchangeNutrition of airways, pleura, vessels
Pressure/resistanceLow (~25/10 mmHg)High (systemic)
FlowWhole cardiac output~1–2% of cardiac output
Response to hypoxiaVasoconstriction (hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction: matches perfusion to ventilation)Vasodilation (like systemic vessels)
Venous returnPulmonary veins → left atriumBronchial veins → azygos/hemiazygos (and some to pulmonary veins)
Links/anastomosesBronchopulmonary anastomoses at capillary/precapillary level and venous drainage of bronchial blood into pulmonary veins (anatomical shunt, ~2% of CO: why normal PaO₂ is slightly lower than alveolar).
Clinical
  • Pulmonary infarction is uncommon after PE because bronchial arteries can maintain tissue viability (infarction more likely with LV failure/lung disease).
  • Massive haemoptysis mostly arises from bronchial arteries (systemic pressure; hypertrophied in bronchiectasis, TB, CF, cancer) → treated by bronchial artery embolisation (risk: spinal artery supply from intercostal/bronchial trunks).
  • Lung transplantation: bronchial arteries usually not reconnected → airway ischaemia at anastomosis.
  • Chronic thromboembolic disease → bronchial collateral hypertrophy.

los.text: Describe the basic conditions predisposing to thrombosis - Virchow's Triad.
los.html:
• Virchow's triad (conditions predisposing to thrombosis):
1. Stasis (abnormal blood flow)
  • Immobility (bed rest, paralysis, long-haul flights)
  • Surgery
  • Heart failure
  • AF (left atrial appendage)
  • Varicose veins
  • Venous obstruction (pregnancy uterus, tumours)
  • Polycythaemia/hyperviscosity
  • Aneurysms (turbulence)
  • Mitral stenosis.
2. Endothelial injury (vessel wall damage)Trauma, surgery, central lines, atherosclerosis (arterial), vasculitis, smoking, hypertension, infection/sepsis, previous DVT (valve damage), chemotherapy.
3. Hypercoagulability (altered blood constituents)
  • Inherited thrombophilia (factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, protein C/S, antithrombin deficiency)
  • Acquired: malignancy
  • Pregnancy/postpartum
  • Oestrogens (COCP, HRT)
  • Antiphospholipid syndrome
  • Nephrotic syndrome (antithrombin loss)
  • IBD
  • Myeloproliferative disease
  • Dehydration
  • Sepsis
  • HIT
  • COVID-19
  • Obesity
  • Smoking.
  • Application: arterial thrombosis is driven mainly by endothelial injury (atherosclerotic plaque rupture: platelet-rich "white" thrombus → antiplatelets)
    • venous thrombosis mainly by stasis + hypercoagulability (fibrin-rich "red" thrombus → anticoagulants)
    • prevention targets each component (mobilisation, compression/IPC, LMWH, line care).

los.text: Be aware of the different types of embolus other than thrombus.
los.html:
• Embolus: a detached intravascular mass (solid, liquid or gas) carried by blood to a site distant from its origin.
    • ~99% are thromboemboli.
TypeCausesFeatures
Fat embolismLong-bone (femur) and pelvic fractures, orthopaedic surgery (intramedullary nailing), liposuction, pancreatitisFat embolism syndrome 24–72 h later: hypoxia/respiratory distress, neurological (confusion), petechial rash (axillae, conjunctivae), thrombocytopenia, retinal fat
Air (gas) embolismCentral line insertion/removal (patient upright, no Valsalva), surgery (neuro sitting position), trauma, decompression sickness (divers: nitrogen bubbles: "the bends"), IV infusionsSudden cardiovascular collapse, breathlessness, neurological signs; >100 mL can be fatal; position left lateral head-down (venous), 100% O₂, hyperbaric O₂
Amniotic fluid embolismLabour/delivery, caesareanSudden hypoxia, hypotension/cardiac arrest, DIC, seizures; high mortality
Septic emboliInfective endocarditis (right-sided → lung abscesses; left-sided → brain, spleen, kidneys), infected thrombophlebitis (Lemierre's)Abscesses, mycotic aneurysms
Tumour emboliRenal cell carcinoma (IVC invasion), atrial myxomaMetastasis, stroke
Cholesterol (atheroembolism)Arterial catheterisation/surgery of atherosclerotic aorta, anticoagulation/thrombolysisLivedo reticularis, blue toes ("trash foot"), AKI, eosinophilia
Foreign materialIV drug use (talc, crushed tablets), catheter fragments, bullets, cement (vertebroplasty)Pulmonary granulomas
Bone marrow/trophoblast/parasites

los.text: Identify structures within the alveolar wall and relate them to function.
los.html:
• Alveolar wall (interalveolar septum) components:
    • Type I pneumocytes: thin, flattened squamous cells covering ~95% of alveolar surface → gas exchange (short diffusion distance); can't divide (damaged in ARDS).
    • Type II pneumocytes: cuboidal cells with lamellar bodies (~5% of surface, ~60% of cells). Secrete surfactant (↓ surface tension, prevents collapse). Progenitors that regenerate type I cells.
    • Alveolar macrophages ("dust cells"): phagocytose particles/microbes; haemosiderin-laden macrophages ("heart failure cells") in chronic congestion.
    • Pulmonary capillaries (continuous endothelium) with fused basement membranes of capillary endothelium and type I cells → blood–air barrier (~0.2–0.6 μm): surfactant/fluid layer, type I cell, fused basement membrane, endothelium.
    • Interstitium: elastic fibres (recoil), collagen, fibroblasts, (myofibroblasts), interstitial fluid, lymphatics near bronchioles.
    • Pores of Kohn (collateral ventilation between alveoli; also route for spread of infection), canals of Lambert.
  • Function and pathology: thin barrier and huge area (~70–100 m²) → efficient diffusion (Fick's law)
    • thickening (fibrosis, oedema) → ↓ diffusion (↓ TLCO, hypoxia)
    • destruction of walls (emphysema) → ↓ surface area and recoil
    • surfactant deficiency (neonatal RDS, ARDS) → collapse
    • fluid in alveoli (oedema, pneumonia) → shunt.
